name: Dana Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Dana, thanks for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both the public version and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Owen Pryce at Greyhill, which is about four hundred ewes on the hill and twenty acres of leeks and cabbages down by the river. Mornings I check the sheep on the quad bike, then it's whatever's urgent, a ewe on her back, a fence the wind took, weeding the brassicas. I'm honestly not very good yet, Owen still laughs at my fencing, but I'm getting faster.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned you're getting faster. What helps?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My phone, mostly. I use an AI app every day, I ask it to plan which field the flock should go on next based on the grass, I get it to draft Owen's movement forms, I even asked it why the cabbages had yellow edges. It's wrong sometimes, so I check, but it's saved me a lot of embarrassment. The bad part is money: I'm on the lowest rate, my partner Mo works shifts at the vegetable packing plant, and we've got less than a month's rent between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's still useful, it just isn't magic. I'd probably post something like 'AI can't put up a fence, who knew'. And then I'd go back to using it for the forms, because it's still quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit disappointed. I was hoping it would make farming less of a grind, maybe even let people like me run a small place one day without a degree. If it stays like this, I'm still the cheapest pair of hands on Owen's farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep learning, keep using the app to get better at the job. I'd try to get Owen to let me run the vegetable side properly, with a plan I make on my phone. Maybe start selling veg boxes on the side if he agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little let down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. Would you keep doing that in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, every day. It's like having an older farmer in your pocket who's read every book but never actually lambed a ewe. You take what it says and then you go and look at the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing big changes, what's your plan for the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get good, get a bit of land on a rented plot, maybe a starter farm from the council if they still do those. I'd want rules that make it possible for someone with no money to start, because right now it's all inherited.

S0.say: It's still useful, it just isn't magic. AI can't put up a fence, who knew. I'll keep using it for the forms because it's quicker.
S0.think: I'm a bit disappointed, because I hoped it would make farming less of a grind and help someone like me run a small place one day. If it stays like this, I'm still the cheapest pair of hands on Owen's farm.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily to plan grazing and draft forms while learning the job. Asks Owen to let her run the vegetable side and considers selling veg boxes on the side.
S0.quote: It's like having an older farmer in your pocket who's read every book but never actually lambed a ewe.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is the rare case who'd be disappointed by the plateau, because she sees AI as a ladder for someone without land or a degree. She uses it daily but checks it against the field. Her progressive view shows in her complaint that farming is mostly inherited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be good if workers get a share, and terrible if they don't. I'd be the one at the young farmers' meeting showing people what the weeding robots can do. And I'd sign anything about making the companies share the profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine for a while, because I'm the one on the farm who actually likes the tech. Owen's 63 and hates his phone. If there's a robot weeding the leeks, someone has to set it up, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now: watch every video, go and see the robot weeder at the trial farm two valleys over, ask the dealer if I can shadow them. I'd push Owen to bring one in on a trial, as long as he agreed I'd run it. I'd look for a short course in farm robotics, online if possible, because I can't afford to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a buzzing way. Excited and a bit sick at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owen's the boss. Would he go along with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble. He'd say his dad weeded leeks by hand. But he's tired and his back's bad, so if I showed him the numbers, he'd come round. Owen likes numbers more than he admits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots owned by the farm. What if they're owned by a company instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be renting my own job back from them. That's the bit that bothers me. I'd want co-ops or the council owning some of them, so small farms aren't held hostage by the subscription.

S1.say: This could be good if workers get a share, and terrible if they don't. Companies should have to share the profits.
S1.think: I'd be fine for a while, because I'm the one on the farm who actually likes the tech. Owen's 63 and hates his phone, so if a robot weeds the leeks, I'm the one who sets it up.
S1.do: Visits the robot weeder trial farm, shadows a dealer and pushes Owen to trial a weeding robot that she would run. Takes a short online course in farm robotics while still working.
S1.feel: Uneasy but buzzing, excited and a little sick together.
S1.quote: Then I'd be renting my own job back from them.
S1.fieldNote: Dana sees steady disruption as her opening, because she's the only person on the farm keen on the technology. Her worry is ownership: she fears renting her own job back from a robot company. She would automate the farm herself, but wants co-op or council ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say we need to pause and share this out before it wrecks everyone. I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for a basic income, and I'd say it loudly online because that's where my generation actually is. I'd also say, to anyone who'd listen, learn this stuff, don't hide from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is too fast even for me. I'm quick with the tech, but if the AI can run the robots too, it doesn't need me to set them up. My advantage only works if there's a gap between the machines and the people, and in this picture the gap closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd try to make some money from what I know, like setting up robots and apps for older farmers round here who are panicking. Cash in hand, while it lasts. I'd join the campaign groups and lean on Mo's family if we needed to, they've got a spare room. And I'd vote for anyone promising a share of the profits for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at 3 a.m. scrolling through news, and I don't usually do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine for a while in the slower picture. Does that hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's the thing. In the slow picture I'm the bridge between Owen and the robot. Here, the robot doesn't need a bridge. I'd have maybe a year of being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mo's at the packing plant. What happens there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The packing plant would go even faster than the farm, it's all lines and boxes. So we'd both be out within the same year. That's what makes it scary, there's no one holding the rope.

S2.say: We need to pause and share this out before it wrecks everyone. Learn this stuff, don't hide from it.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for me. My advantage is being the bridge between the old farmers and the machines, and here the gap closes before I can use it.
S2.do: Sets up robots and apps for panicking older farmers for cash while it lasts. Joins basic income campaigns, votes for profit-sharing, and leans on Mo's family's spare room if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at 3 a.m. scrolling the news.
S2.quote: In the slow picture I'm the bridge between Owen and the robot. Here, the robot doesn't need a bridge.
S2.fieldNote: Even adaptive Dana gets alarmed here: her edge depends on a gap between machines and people, and two years closes it. She'd still act fast, turning her skills into cash work for older farmers. Both her and Mo's jobs would go in the same year, which removes their safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, let's not waste them arguing. I'd want the council setting up a robot co-op for small farms, and I'd go to the meetings to say so. Online I'd share what I'm learning so other farmhands don't get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives me a real run, three or four good years of being the person who makes the robots work. After that, maybe nothing. But I'd go into 2031 with skills and contacts instead of just a quad bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do the farm robotics course properly and get Owen's leek robot in. I'd keep learning on the AI every day. I'd try to put money aside, even a hundred a month, which would be a first for me. And I'd help start a co-op with three or four other farms so we own the machines together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which is better than the alternative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long do you think you'd be the bridge, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, three or four years. After that the AI runs the robots itself and the bridge gets knocked down. So I'd be using those years to build something that doesn't depend on being the bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deposit, maybe, on a few acres and a polytunnel. Or a stake in the co-op. Something that's mine, so when the work goes, I've got land and a share of the machines, not just a payslip that's stopped.

S3.say: We've got five years, let's not waste them arguing. The council should set up a robot co-op for small farms.
S3.think: It gives me three or four good years as the person who makes the robots work, and after that maybe nothing. But I'd go into 2031 with skills and contacts instead of just a quad bike.
S3.do: Completes a farm robotics course and gets a leek robot in at Greyhill. Starts saving a hundred a month and helps set up a co-op with three or four farms to own machines together.
S3.quote: Something that's mine, so when the work goes, I've got land and a share of the machines, not just a payslip that's stopped.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Dana thinks in terms of ownership rather than employment: land, a polytunnel, a share of the machines. She knows her bridge role has an end date and plans past it. Her progressive outlook turns into a practical co-op plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to do it fairly. Ten years is enough to change the law so robots pay into the system the way workers do. I'd be campaigning for that, and I'd tell the young farmers to learn the machines now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd actually do all right, as long as the money gets shared. Ten years is enough to get qualified, get some land, maybe help run a co-op. It's the same end point, but I'd be meeting it as an owner, not a farmhand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, same as before: the course, the leek robot, the co-op. But I'd also go for a proper qualification, two years part-time at the agricultural college, so I'm not just the girl who's good with phones. I'd save, and I'd get involved in local politics, maybe the parish council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. I'd feel like I had a fair shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra five years, compared with the last picture, buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land. Five years isn't enough to save for anything, but ten might be, especially if I share with others. And a real qualification, which means people take me seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that worries you more than five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people would get lazy. Ten years sounds like forever, so the government does nothing for eight of them. I'd be worried I'd do my part and still get caught by everyone else not doing theirs.

S4.say: This is the chance to do it fairly. Ten years is enough to change the law so robots pay into the system the way workers do.
S4.think: I'd actually do all right as long as the money gets shared. It's the same end point, but I'd meet it as an owner, not a farmhand.
S4.do: Studies part-time for two years at the agricultural college on top of the robotics course and co-op work. Saves towards land and joins local politics, perhaps the parish council.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, with a fair shot.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever, so the government does nothing for eight of them.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Dana picture herself as an owner rather than a worker, which is what changes her mood. Her remaining fear is political: that everyone else wastes the time. She shows how a progressive, adaptive person turns warning time into both training and campaigning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan is being the bridge and there'd be no time to cross it. What would help is robots owned by co-ops and councils, not just big companies, and some kind of basic income while people retrain. Also starter farms, land you can rent cheaply, so people like me can own something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the sheep. The robots can maybe weed leeks, but a ewe stuck in a bog on the hill in February, I'd like to see the robot do that. I'm not sure that last bit of the job ever goes, and nobody's planning for it.

headlineQuote: a ewe stuck in a bog on the hill in February, I'd like to see the robot do that.
portrait: Dana Chen is 27 and works for Owen Pryce at Greyhill, a hill sheep and vegetable farm, living with her partner Mo, who works at a packing plant, on less than a month's savings. She uses an AI app every day and is the only person on the farm keen on new technology. She is a little disappointed by the AI Plateau, sees Steady Disruption as her chance, and is alarmed only when AGI comes in two years and leaves no time to be the bridge between old farmers and the machines. With more warning, she plans for ownership: a robotics course, a farm co-op, and saving for land. Her politics are about who owns the robots and who shares the profits.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her plan depends on being the bridge to the machines and there would be no time to cross it.
whatWouldHelp: Robots owned by co-ops and councils rather than only big companies, a basic income while people retrain, and cheap starter farms so people like her can own something.
